Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-04] Learner-facing language follows the course setting. For the first course (UPSC / State PCS) it is Hinglish: natural Hindi sentence flow, English technical terms, the way Navin teaches.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S2-01] Plan the chapter's videos from the chapter map: first one short 'pehle yeh jaan lo' video (5-8 minutes) that teaches the chapter's prerequisites, then the topic videos in teaching order. Narration is 6-8 minutes per book page (Navin, 23 October 2026; the 14-page tissue chapter about 85-110 minutes of topic videos, plus the prerequisite video): each topic video gets the share of the pages its items come from, and a very dense page may go up to 25% over when the plan says why. Understanding (Section 1) and the chapter map have no time limit.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the result first (what it makes). 2) inputs and the place. 3) each step with its cause and its condition. 4) what breaks when a step fails. 5) the whole run once more at speed. 6) recap as a flow.
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the whole in context. 2) zoom into each part in a fixed path (outside to inside). 3) function of each part tied to its shape. 4) how the parts work together. 5) labelled recap.
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the overview tree first: the basis of division and every member named. 2) every member in the same slots: layer and shape, why it is named so, its special feature, its function with its cause, where it is found by a zoom from the organ, its consequence. 3) the members compared side by side, the most confused pair named directly. 4) a memory trick for the family.
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
  Teaching pattern: 1) what is common. 2) criteria one at a time, both sides together. 3) the reason behind each difference. 4) the most confused pair named directly. 5) difference table as recap.
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the period and its atmosphere. 2) events in order with their causes. 3) the people and their choices. 4) the turning point. 5) what changed after. 6) timeline recap.
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the effect students can see. 2) the cause. 3) each link of the chain with its mechanism. 4) the evidence. 5) the exception or limit. 6) the chain as recap.
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
  Teaching pattern: 1) the fact in one line. 2) the number shown to scale against something familiar. 3) where it comes from (book or outside, dated). 4) what it changes or proves. 5) a formula built term by term when there is one.
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
  Teaching pattern: 1) what the figure is and why it is here. 2) a reading path across it (labels in order). 3) the one thing to remember from it. 4) link back to the text it explains.
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).
  Teaching pattern: 1) a concrete example first. 2) the book's definition word by word. 3) a non-example that tests the boundary. 4) where the term is used next in the chapter.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-29.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- Open with a question on something visible (every new topic and every new family member): Skin aur stomach, kidney ke upar ek outer layer hai ki nahi? Yeh kis se bani hai? — phir naam: epithelial tissue.
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Contrast with the neighbour (members of one family, and what the exam confuses): Simple epithelium ka kaam protection nahi, woh compound ka hai. Zyada layers = pathogen andar nahi aata.
- Ask and repeat the key word (the one word the learner must keep): Irregular walls. Kaisi? Irregular.
- Exam memory beats by level (after the understanding, by the level profile): Yaad rakhna: brush border PCT mein. Doosre naam: pavement, tessellated. M2B = muscle to bone = tendon, B2B = bone to bone = ligament.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. p003-i13 | 3 | definition | definition | • Metallic money is made from metals such as gold, silver, copper, bronze, or electrum, whose value is derived from the metal itself and, later, from the authority that minted it.
  p003-i13#q1 | what | What is metallic money, and which materials are named? → It is money made from metals such as gold, silver, copper, bronze or electrum. The page connects its value first to the metal and later also to the minting authority. | book

  p003-i13#q3 | how | How can minting authority help a metal object function as money? → A recognized issuer's mark can support confidence in stated weight, purity or denomination, reducing the need for each trader to assess an unmarked metal piece. | outside
  p003-i13#q4 | what | What do bronze, electrum and minted mean here? → Bronze is chiefly a copper-tin alloy; electrum is a gold-silver alloy. Minting means making and issuing coins, usually with identifying marks. | outside

beats.say: कुछ सिक्के ले जाना आसान है; हजारों साथ ले जाने हों, तो क्या होगा?
beats.on_screen: Small coin pouch versus a large coin load.

beats.say: अनाज वाला यह coin क्यों लेगा? मान लो, पहले उसके पास 0 silver coins थे; आपने अनाज के बदले 1 दिया, उसने metal और पहचानी छाप देखकर स्वीकार किया।
beats.on_screen: Illustrative grain purchase: seller initially has no silver coins; buyer hands over 1 recognized silver coin for grain.

beats.say: यह Metallic money है: gold, silver, copper, bronze या electrum का पैसा। Bronze ज़्यादातर copper–tin का alloy है; electrum में gold–silver मिलते हैं, यानी metals का मिला रूप।
beats.on_screen: Metallic money: five listed materials. Separate explanatory inset: bronze chiefly copper–tin; electrum gold–silver.
beats.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition, entries Bronze and Electrum, 1911.

beats.say: Value पहले metal से, बाद में minting authority से भी जुड़ी। Minted यानी सिक्का बनाकर जारी किया; पहचान वाली छाप वजन और purity पर भरोसा देती है, इसलिए बार-बार जाँच घटती है।
beats.on_screen: Core claim: metal value and minting authority. Explanatory inset: issuer mark supports confidence in specifications.
beats.source: W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapters V and VII, 1875.

beats.say: Metal का spoon पैसा नहीं है। Coin की face value भी उसके metal की कीमत के बराबर जरूरी नहीं।
beats.on_screen: Metal object ≠ necessarily money. Face value need not equal metal value.
beats.source: W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapters VII and VIII, 1875.

beats.say: यानी metal के साथ issuer की पहचान भी मायने रखती है।
beats.on_screen: Metal value + issuer recognition.

beats.say: Payment में 20 kg अनाज ढोना आसान होगा? मान लो, seller ने उसकी जगह सिक्के स्वीकार किए; आपने सिक्के दिए और अनाज बिल्कुल नहीं ढोया।
beats.on_screen: Hypothetical payment: instead of carrying 20 kg of grain, buyer pays accepted coins and carries no grain. Not a historical exchange rate.

beats.say: यही portability है: कीमत ले जाना आसान; standardization यानी coins की तय पहचान। Intrinsic value metal की अपनी कीमत है। आपने 1 coin कई बार चलाया, फिर भी वह जल्दी खराब नहीं हुआ; यही durability है।
beats.on_screen: Portable pouch; agreed specifications; metal's own value. Illustrative repeated-use sequence: one coin passes through several payments and remains usable → durability.
beats.source: W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapters V and VI, 1875.

beats.say: ₹10 देने हों, आपने ₹5 के 2 coins दिए; यही divisibility है, छोटे denominations से रकम बाँटना, coin काटना नहीं। तय पहचान से जाँच घटती है; widespread acceptance से लेने वाला खोजना आसान होता है, इसलिए व्यापार ज्यादा भरोसेमंद बनता है।
beats.on_screen: Illustrative payment: buyer owes ₹10 and hands over two ₹5 coins. Then reveal divisibility. Standardization → less checking; acceptance → easier exchange.
beats.source: W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapters III, V and VII, 1875.

beats.say: Mandi में खरीद बढ़े तो? पहले व्यापारी ने 100 coins दिए थे; अब ज्यादा अनाज खरीदने के लिए 1000 देने हैं। इतना बोझ उठाना और चोरी से बचाना मुश्किल होगा।
beats.on_screen: Hypothetical merchant previously pays 100 coins; larger grain purchase now requires 1000 at unchanged coin value. Show porter and guarded coin load.

beats.say: ये scale और transport limitations हैं। Limited supply यानी खरीद बढ़ते ही नया metal नहीं मिलता; payment के साधन बढ़ाना मुश्किल होता है।
beats.on_screen: Growing purchases face limited monetary metal; larger payments require heavier loads.
beats.source: W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapters V and XVI, 1875.

beats.say: घिसा coin देखा? Wear and tear से वजन या छाप घटती है। अब मान लो, उसी denomination के coin में पहले 10 gram silver था; बनाने वाले ने जानबूझकर सिर्फ 8 gram रखा। यह coin debasement है: बताई कीमत के मुकाबले कीमती metal घटाना, अपने-आप घिसना नहीं।
beats.on_screen: Wear: repeated handling erodes metal or marks. Separate hypothetical example: unchanged denomination; maker replaces 10 g silver content with 8 g → deliberate debasement. Not historical coin specifications.
beats.source: W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapters VIII and XIII, 1875.

beats.say: कम metal, भारी ढुलाई, चोरी और coin की quality की मुश्किलों ने बड़े व्यापार को संभालना कठिन बनाया; इसलिए paper money अपनाने की जरूरत बनी।
beats.on_screen: Limited supply + transport + theft + wear/debasement → constraints on expanding trade → adoption of paper money.

beats.say: Paper भी चोरी हो सकता है। Gold देने का वादा हो, तो paper जारी करते समय वह वादा निभाने की क्षमता चाहिए।
beats.on_screen: Paper does not eliminate theft. Gold-convertible paper remains subject to fulfilling conversion promises.
beats.source: W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapter XVI, 1875.

beats.say: कड़ी पकड़ो: आसान payment, बढ़ता व्यापार, फिर metal की सीमाओं से paper की जरूरत।
beats.on_screen: Convenient metallic payments → expanding trade → metal's limitations → paper alternatives.

beats.say: तौला metal और तय पहचान वाला coin एक हैं? हर अलग टुकड़े की जाँच करनी पड़ सकती थी।
beats.on_screen: Metal piece on scales beside recognizable standardized coin.
beats.source: W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapters V and VII, 1875.

beats.say: Mesopotamia और Egypt में शुरुआती metallic exchange objects थे, यानी metal देकर खरीदना। First standardized coins आम तौर पर Kingdom of Lydia से जुड़े हैं; दोनों शुरुआतें अलग रखो।
beats.on_screen: Mesopotamia and Egypt: early metallic exchange objects. Lydia: widely credited first standardized coins.

beats.say: Standardized यानी तय वजन, बनावट या पहचान: अलग-अलग टुकड़ों के बजाय पहचाने जाने वाले coins।
beats.on_screen: Irregular metal pieces → coins with agreed specifications.
beats.source: W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapter VII, 1875.

beats.say: इससे हर payment में जाँच की मेहनत घट सकती थी।
beats.on_screen: Recognizable coin specifications → reduced repeated assessment.
beats.source: W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapter VII, 1875.

beats.say: याद रखो: Mesopotamia–Egypt में metal exchange; Lydia में standardized coins।
beats.on_screen: Two separate historical associations.

beats.say: Indian coins की कतार कैसे पढ़ोगे? बाएँ से दाएँ, ऊपर समय या dynasty, नीचे जुड़ी coinage देखो।
beats.on_screen: Five connected circular markers; period above, coin description below.

beats.say: छोटे दबे निशान कैसे बने? Punch-marked में punch से निशान लगते हैं; पहला पड़ाव 6th c. BCE है, यानी छठी century, एक साल नहीं।
beats.on_screen: 6th c. BCE / Punch-marked; animate punch impressions.

beats.say: अगला silver coin किससे जुड़ा है? Mauryan–Imperial silver, यानी empire से जुड़ी silver coinage; Mauryan को Ashoka की Maurya dynasty से पहचानो।
beats.on_screen: Second marker: Mauryan / Imperial silver. Historical-context inset, distinct from timeline pairing: Ashoka → Maurya dynasty.
beats.source: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, chapter 2, 2007.

beats.say: Design कैसे पड़ा? तीसरा Indo-Greek–Die-struck: design वाले die की चोट metal पर छाप छोड़ती है; यह technique है, metal नहीं। Indo-Greek उत्तर-पश्चिम में Greek-origin rulers थे।
beats.on_screen: Third pairing: Indo-Greek / Die-struck. Separate context insets: northwestern subcontinent and Greek-origin rulers; engraved die strikes metal blank.
beats.source: R. S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, 2005; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition, Numismatics, 1911.

beats.say: सोने के coins का नाम क्या है? चौथा Gupta–Gold dinars: dinar नाम के gold coins; Gupta को Chandragupta II की dynasty से जोड़ो।
beats.on_screen: Fourth pairing: Gupta / Gold dinars. Separate historical-context inset: Chandragupta II → Gupta dynasty.
beats.source: R. S. Sharma, India's Ancient Past, 2005.

beats.say: आखिरी silver coin का नाम? 1540 CE–Rupiya, Sher Shah Suri से जुड़ा standardized silver coin; आज के rupee जैसा metal या purchasing power मत मानना।
beats.on_screen: Final pairing: 1540 CE / Rupiya. Separate historical-context inset: Sher Shah Suri; standardized silver coin. Historical and modern coins are not identical specifications.
beats.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition, Rupee, 1911; W. Stanley Jevons, Money and the Mechanism of Exchange, chapter VIII, 1875.

beats.say: Matching में association है, ‘केवल यही’ नहीं। बराबर gaps बराबर समय नहीं: century, dynasty और 1540 CE जैसा खास साल अलग labels हैं।
beats.on_screen: Read associations, not exclusivity. Schematic spacing is not elapsed time. Century ≠ dynasty ≠ specific year.

beats.say: क्रम याद रखो: Punch-marked, Mauryan silver, Indo-Greek Die-struck, Gupta dinars, 1540 का Rupiya; याद का सहारा: निशान, silver, technique, gold, Rupiya।
